I think this course is fun overall, especially if you like music. However, the final project being done with groups was a bit difficult to manage I think. There can be another option added other than of fieldwork or music composition project; like a through research paper about a topic relating to class; which we can do individually.

The course spent only two hours on Turkish music, completely skipping Turkish pop and rock. Even Turkish art music was rushed, while five weeks were dedicated to electronic music and synthesizers. This is surprising, considering we are Bilkent students living in Ankara. While global knowledge is important, we are Turkish, and many of us even play instruments. Our own music deserves more attention.

The instructor often uses obscure song examples with very few YouTube views (10K at most) and repeatedly asks, "Do you know this?" No, we don’t—this is why we’re here. These examples are irrelevant, as they are neither classical nor folk music and are barely known even in their countries of origin. Why not use examples from Turkey or popular songs that we can relate to? The lectures feel unstructured and disconnected.

We were also made to watch documentaries in class that were only loosely related to the topics, further adding to the confusion.

The workload for this course sometimes felt like too much. There are 7 assignments you need to do throughout the semester, but these are spread out so evenly that you have to do some of them in your busiest weeks. I wish the course was designed so that our final dates, etc. are taken into account. 
Other than that, I found the attendance requirements to be a little strict.
Also, the midterm exam was quite difficult, although I was careful enough to take notes all the time and make a revision. I felt the questions were too broad, and it is quite difficult to know what to study because there really is so much being covered. More guidance on the exam topics would have been better.
Apart from that, the course is an excellent introduction to music in all its forms, and I highly recommend to anyone interested

The instructor was relatively rude, answering questions in class with a strict “No” or “Never” and offering no further explanation. She also showed a poor understanding of student psychology, as illustrated by the following example: the uploaded “sample” midterm came from a completely different course, while the actual midterm was drawn from another source. Students were essentially tricked into studying for an exam that had no relation to the real one.
When we asked the instructor about this, she replied, “Yeah, it was my mistake that I uploaded it; I should not have uploaded it.” In truth, she could have created an exam that even remotely resembled the sample midterm, allowing us to prepare more effectively and gain a better grasp of the course topics.

The instructor also misused make up hours, giving only two days’ notice and disrupting the weekly plans many of us had already made.

The description of this course is as follows:
“The Culture and Basics of Music Making focuses on the definitions, compositional techniques, performance practices and the structural materials of the music's foremost genres. The course offers a broad perspective that features an eclectic scope of distinct historical and cultural contexts in order to convey a core comprehension of the fundaments of music making process. Many different styles will be discussed including but not limited to: Classical Music, pop music, jazz, funk, electronic music, song, concerto, opera, madrigal, symphony, ballet.”

Although we discussed every one of these styles, we did more than simply cover them—we dissected each piece as if we were music department majors. The exams were graded extremely harshly, with comments such as, “The answer is just slightly correct; it’s not entirely correct, so I cannot give you any marks.”
